unit.title: Distribution and the customer journey
unit.description: Direct and indirect channels, intensive, selective and exclusive distribution, marketplaces, omnichannel, touchpoints

cards.definition: The path a product takes to the customer. Direct: the brand sells itself (site, own shops). Indirect: through intermediaries such as wholesalers, retailers or marketplaces, who take a margin in exchange for reach.
cards.example: Nespresso sells in its own boutiques and site (direct) and its machines in electronics stores (indirect).

cards.definition: Intensive: everywhere possible (soda, gum). Selective: a chosen network of retailers (good electronics, cosmetics). Exclusive: a few outlets per area, often for luxury or high-service products.
cards.example: Coca-Cola is intensive; Apple products in approved resellers are selective; a Ferrari dealer per region is exclusive.

cards.definition: A platform where third-party sellers sell to buyers in exchange for a commission (Amazon, Cdiscount, Vinted, Back Market). Huge reach, but the platform owns the customer relationship and the data.
cards.example: A small brand sells on Amazon for volume and pushes repeat buyers to its own site with a card in the parcel.

cards.definition: Tension between the channels of a brand, for example when its own website undercuts the retailers who distribute it. It must be managed with prices, exclusive ranges or shared revenue.
cards.example: Retailers stop pushing a brand after it sells online 20 percent cheaper than them.

exercises.prompt: A brand sells only through its own website and shops. What kind of distribution is it?
exercises.explain: Direct distribution keeps the margin and the customer data, but the brand must build its own reach.

exercises.prompt: Chewing gum is sold in supermarkets, kiosks, stations and vending machines. Which distribution intensity?
exercises.explain: Impulse products need maximum physical availability: intensive distribution.

exercises.prompt: A luxury watchmaker allows one dealer per big city. Which distribution intensity?
exercises.explain: Exclusive distribution protects the image and the service level, at the cost of reach.

exercises.prompt: What is the main downside of selling through a marketplace like Amazon?
choices: The platform owns the customer relationship and data
It is impossible to reach many buyers there
The platform never takes a commission
exercises.explain: Reach is the upside; the cost is a commission and limited access to your own customers. Smart brands use it as an entry door.

exercises.prompt: Buy online, pick up in store, and return in any shop: which approach is this?
exercises.explain: Omnichannel links the channels so the customer moves between them seamlessly. Multichannel only runs several channels side by side.

exercises.prompt: A brand sells on its website 20 percent cheaper than its retailers. What risk does it create?
choices: Channel conflict: retailers stop pushing the brand
Better relations with all its retail partners
A rise of its prices in the shops
No risk: customers never compare prices
exercises.explain: Retailers bring reach; undercutting them pushes them to favour competitors. Brands manage it with price parity or exclusive products.

exercises.prompt: A touchpoint is any moment where a customer meets the brand: an ad, a review, a delivery, a call to support.
exercises.explain: True. A journey map lists the touchpoints and the emotions at each one, to fix the moments that make people drop out.

exercises.prompt: A buyer sees an ad, reads reviews, visits the shop, then orders online. Why map this journey?
choices: To find where people drop out and fix those moments
To credit the whole sale to the last click
To remove every channel except the shop
To prove that ads have no effect at all
exercises.explain: Mapping the journey shows friction and missing information. It also reminds you that the last click is rarely the whole story.

exercises.prompt: What does physical availability mean for Byron Sharp?
choices: Being easy to find and buy, everywhere buyers look
Having a big warehouse full of stock
Opening a flagship store in Paris
Always selling at the lowest price
exercises.explain: Physical availability (with mental availability) is one of the two drivers of brand growth: be present wherever and whenever people buy the category.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the classic indirect path of a consumer product.
exercises.explain: Each intermediary takes a margin and adds a service: storage, logistics, display, advice. Direct sales skip some of these steps.
